text: Every table in a ServiceNow instance already has a working REST API the moment the table exists. No sys_ws_definition record, no Resource, no script. This is the Table API — the platform's built-in, automatic REST interface to the same data GlideRecord reads and writes server-side.

The base path is /api/now/table/ followed by the table name, and the HTTP method decides the operation. GET with no sys_id lists records; GET with a sys_id returns exactly one. POST creates, PUT or PATCH updates, DELETE removes. Swap in any table name — incident, a custom table, anything — and the same six operations just work.

An unfiltered list GET would try to return every record in the table. sysparm_query takes an encoded query — the exact same syntax GlideRecord's addQuery and addEncodedQuery build server-side, just written as a query string. The caret joins conditions with AND. If you've already read an encoded query inside a Business Rule, you already know how to read this.

Two more parameters shape the response itself. sysparm_fields is a comma-separated list — only those fields get serialized per record, instead of every field on the table. sysparm_limit caps how many records come back in one call, which matters for paging through a large result set. Every response wraps its payload in a top-level result key.

The Table API's whole advantage is that it's automatic, and that's also its limit. It mirrors a table's raw fields with no custom logic in between — it can't validate an incoming payload beyond the table's own ACLs and Business Rules, it can't reshape a response into a format an external system expects, and it can't combine data from more than one table into a single response. That's exactly where a Scripted REST API takes over — anywhere the integration needs transformation, aggregation, or custom validation logic.
The Table API covers the simple case instantly. Next, Scripted REST APIs get a developer's-depth look — going well past the fundamentals-level build from course six.
